title: NAVIGATING THROUGH PAUL'S LETTERS: WALKING THROUGH GALATIANS

sense.text:
Israel brought “the shewbread”, “the continual meat offering”, “the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts”, and “the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel”. Making an atonement for Israel: atonement, reconciliation and justification for Israel are all the same thing, the same reconciliation of Israel that Romans 5 goes into.

“And for all the work of the house of our God.” That is the works. All the work of the house of our God: the sacrifices, the sin offerings, the burnt offerings, temple law.

This is the answer given first, before Galatians is opened. When Paul writes of the works of the law, it is the works of the law, singular, not the works of the laws: the law of sacrifice, what was offered at the house of God to make an atonement for Israel. It stands behind Galatians 2:16, 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10. There are many others like it; Nehemiah 10:33 is simply convenient.

Peter calls him “our beloved brother Paul”, who wrote “according to the wisdom given unto him”. Wisdom is not a what but a who: Christ is wisdom, and Christ is the wisdom that was given to Paul. By that wisdom he “hath written unto you” concerning our salvation and the longsuffering of our Lord.

“As also in all his epistles”: Peter read all of Paul's letters. He never said, this is off but I'll let it slide and let it spread. If Paul wrote things that were off, it implicates Peter. If it implicates Peter, it implicates James; if James, then John, the last surviving disciple, who never wrote against Paul. Say one stupid thing and everything else sounds more stupid: disregard and disrespect Paul and you put all the remaining disciples into heresy, and make Christ a negligent Messiah who sat back quiet while Paul filled letters with error, then waited thousands of years to send someone down to say Paul was wrong. So Peter shows that Paul's letters were inspired through Paul by the wisdom of Christ, and they are credible.

In them “are some things hard to be understood”. A lot of what Paul wrote is complex and very difficult, especially for those who are not keeping God's commandments, and that is why these lessons walk through his letters.

“Which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest”. The unlearned don't study, or are not taught by the right teachers. The unstable find fault in Paul's letters because they don't really believe what the Bible says. To wrest is to wrestle with it, to fight with it, to twist it: to make Paul say something other than what he wrote. “As they do also the other scriptures”: the other scriptures are the Old Testament, the law and the prophets, which they are just as unlearned and unstable in, and twist “unto their own destruction.”

“Beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness.” Don't fall from your steadfast belief in the validity of Paul's writings because of the error of the wicked. The error of the wicked takes Paul's letters and says all nations can be saved; that Paul grafted the other nations in; that we can commit adultery; that the Sabbath day is changed; that we don't have to keep the laws anymore. All of that is the error of the wicked.

precepts.why:
Paul says it himself: “I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come”. When Paul wrote his letters, his primary reference was none other than what Moses and the prophets wrote. That was his source material: the source of Paul's letters was the law and the prophets.

Paul's letters predate the gospels, with the exception of Mark. Most agree Mark's gospel is the oldest. Mark, Luke and Matthew are called the synoptic gospels, meaning they all see the same thing, and Matthew and Luke are said to have borrowed from Mark, because Mark was Peter's scribe. That is why Peter has no gospel: Mark is Peter's gospel. And it makes sense that Mark's gospel is the oldest, because Peter's and Paul's ministries were at the same time. Paul's letters range from the 40s AD to the 60s AD; John's gospel was written around 90 AD, and Revelation 95 to 100 AD.

So the other scriptures that the unlearned and unstable wrest along with Paul are the very scriptures Paul built his letters on.

In his lodging Paul “expounded and testified the kingdom of God, persuading them concerning Jesus, both out of the law of Moses, and out of the prophets, from morning till evening.” That is the other scriptures. His source material was the Old Testament.

Paul was not pulling from John 3:16, because when Paul wrote his letters there was no John 3:16 at all. John wrote that gospel around 90 AD, twenty years after the besieging of Jerusalem by Rome in 70 AD. Paul was not quoting John, Matthew or Luke; his letters predate them. Luke was travelling with him while he wrote. Luke wrote Luke and Luke wrote Acts: Acts is basically a second Luke, Luke's letter number two.

So Paul is read by the law and the prophets, because that is what he read from.

sense.text: Christ “gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world”. These are possessive words: our sins, deliver us. Christians read that and say everyone. It does not say everyone. It says our.

“I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel”. Paul ran into an issue with the Galatians: they were being deceived and manipulated by people coming into the church and spreading confusion.

“Which is not another”: they were being moved by a gospel which is not another, because the troublers used the same books. “There be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ.” At that time it was the Pharisees and Sadducees. Today it is Christian pastors, and Israelites who are slowly seeping back into Christianity's cult doctrine.

“Let him be accursed”: let him be destroyed.

The gospel is the good news for Israelites: the good news of our deliverance, our salvation. The Messiah is a black man who died for the sins of his people and his people alone. That is gospel. Us being in America temporarily and getting divine reparations and justice: that is good news, that is gospel.

When you try to include your enemies in that, that is another gospel. People ask what is wrong with teaching the nations to be saved, what is the danger in it. The danger is you get accursed, because you include your enemy in a salvation, in good news, that does not belong to them. It is like delivering the newspaper to the wrong house, or taking your food to somebody else's house: it doesn't belong to them, it belongs to you. Telling the nations a gospel that does not apply to them, the Bible says you are accursed. An inclusive gospel is another gospel.

The Bible is an exclusive salvation, not an inclusive one. That is why the Roman Catholic Church was formed: the word Catholic itself means inclusive. God calls us a peculiar people, and when you are peculiar you are not inclusive, you are exclusive: separate from everybody else, different.

Paul is not writing things down based on his feelings and emotions. “The gospel which was preached of me is not after man. For I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ.” Christ taught him, and Peter said the same: the wisdom given unto him. Christ gave him that wisdom, and Peter confirmed it in his letter. Even where Paul gives advice, like wishing that all would stay single as he was, but if you cannot, then get married, even in that is the spirit of the Lord talking to him.

Paul “profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals in mine own nation”. Paul came from a very well-off, very prestigious family of Pharisees. His father was a Pharisee and he was raised one, educated under Gamaliel. He profited in the Jews' religion, Judaism, the Mosaic law, which at this time was against Christ. He excelled above many, “being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers.”

God “separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me by his grace”. The Lord had already predestined Paul to be the man he became. For all the persecution, the killings and the harm he did to the church, Paul learned later that the Lord had called him from birth and that he had a purpose.

“To reveal his Son in me”: in Paul. That goes back to what Peter said, the wisdom given unto him. Christ was speaking through Paul. So when Paul's letters say the Lord says, the error of the wicked says that is just his opinion, his thoughts. No: that is Christ speaking through Paul. Paul is not held above Christ, but we know when Christ is speaking through Paul. Many refuse to acknowledge it, because they are like the people in this same chapter who preach another gospel, so they can violate Christ, do what they want, teach who they want to teach and make the money they want to make.

“That I might preach him among the heathen”. Why the heathen? Because Israelites were among the heathen.

Paul “communicated unto them that gospel which I preach among the Gentiles”. Among the heathen, among the Gentiles: Paul keeps using that word among, because Israel was scattered among the nations. That is who he is talking to the entire time he writes letters: those among the nations.

“But privately to them which were of reputation”. Paul would teach those he knew were of reputation, those he could trust, and go into deep things with them, “lest by any means I should run, or had run, in vain”: lest he teach the wrong people.
Titus is called “a Greek”. Who the Greeks were is unfolded later, at Galatians 3:28: Israelites who had been made Greeks.

“False brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage”. Keep the liberty and the bondage in mind; they are unfolded through the letter. The liberty is that Christ's death freed us from having to atone with animals: we are no longer obligated to offer up animals for our sins. The bondage is being brought back under that.

“To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour”: Paul paid them no mind. In other words, to hell with them. “That the truth of the gospel might continue with you”, because these men were preaching against it.

“Who seemed to be somewhat”: they had some reputation. People knew them; they had a school, a group, they were part of a camp. “Whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me”: Paul is saying, I don't give a damn who they are. “God accepteth no man’s person”, and they “added nothing to me.”

“But contrariwise”: aside from these insignificant negroes. The disciples saw “that the gospel of the uncircumcision was committed unto me, as the gospel of the circumcision was unto Peter”. Those among the heathen, among the Gentiles, Paul calls the uncircumcision.

“He that wrought effectually in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision”: Christ wrought effectually in Peter, toward the Jews born and raised in the law, who are called the circumcision. “The same was mighty in me toward the Gentiles”: the same Christ. The spirit of Christ that worked effectually in Peter toward the circumcised worked the same way in Paul toward the uncircumcised, those among the Gentiles.

James, Cephas and John “perceived the grace that was given unto me”: the spirit of Christ, wisdom. “That we should go unto the heathen”, another word for Gentile, the Israelites among the nations, “and they unto the circumcision”: the Jews that were not scattered abroad.

“When Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.” Antioch is Turkey, and Galatia is Turkey, a Turkish area. Peter went off a little, and Paul confronted him about it.

Before certain came from James, Peter “did eat with the Gentiles”: he sat down and taught the Israelites scattered abroad, who were deemed Gentiles. “But when they were come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing them which were of the circumcision”, the Jews. He got nervous and acted like he wasn't with them. “The other Jews dissembled likewise with him”: they pretended too, ashamed to be seen among them, because their faith was not built up yet, “insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation.”

“If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?” Paul is asking why Peter is being a poor example: if you want them to live as us and keep God's commandments, why pretend they are not our people? “We who are Jews by nature, and not sinners of the Gentiles”: Paul calls these Gentiles sinners. Peter's job was to go out and teach them who they are, the Bible and repentance. You can't pull them in by acting like you're not with them when the Jews come around.

“Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ”. Here is where the other gospel comes in, the corruption, the error of the wicked. They say, see, no one is justified by the works of the law; all you have to do is believe; you don't have to keep any laws; you can lie, cheat, steal and rape in the name of Jesus. A Christian once said exactly that, a crazy Dominican in the Bronx: yes, according to the Bible, in the name of Christ you can rape. A stupid Dominican, dumb as hell.

The answer was given at the start, with Nehemiah 10:33. The works are the sacrifices, the sin offerings, the burnt offerings, temple law, all the work of the house of our God. It says the works of the law, law singular. The law meant is the law of sacrifice. A man is no longer justified, no longer receives atonement or reconciliation, by sacrificial law, but “by the faith of Christ”. “For by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.”

This ties back to Romans 5, where justification, atonement and reconciliation were opened with Isaiah 45:25 and Isaiah 53:11: Paul was a genius, and it all goes together. Galatians 2:16 is one of the Christians' go-to verses, and every place Paul says the works of the law it goes into the same thing.

precepts.why:
“Then said the Jews among themselves”. The Jews here are the circumcision: all born and raised in Mosaic law and circumcised the eighth day by law. The Jews who were not born and raised in the law were called the uncircumcision.

“Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles”: where will Christ go that we cannot find him? The dispersed are the Israelites, the diaspora. Among the Gentiles: the same words Paul keeps writing, among the heathen, among the Gentiles. And then: “and teach the Gentiles?” The dispersed Israelites are themselves called Gentiles.

So now you know who the Gentiles are that Paul is writing to throughout the entire time: the Israelites scattered among the nations. That is the uncircumcision toward whom Christ was mighty in Paul, as he wrought effectually in Peter toward the circumcision.

sense.text:
The works of the law is the law of sacrifice, the use of animals. Christ's death freed us from having to atone with animals: that is the liberty spied out in Galatians 2. Otherwise we are condemned, because the temple is gone and the priests are scattered, stupid and lost, so we can't atone that way.

If you seek to be justified by animals, you are a condemned man, because there are sins no animal can cover. If you were out here selling drugs, weed, psychedelics, LSD, cocaine, crack, you were a witch, a sorcerer: that is death. If you are a pimp, you are a whoremonger: death for that too. There is no atoning for witchcraft. So those who came from that background, thank Christ for dying for you; otherwise your ass would be finished. Idolatry: done. Catholic, condemned. Baptist, condemned. Muslim, condemned. Say you're still under the old covenant, and you're done, because you need an animal and a priest to atone, and there is no animal for that.

And you are not David, you are not Moses, you are not Solomon; you don't get the pass they did. The exception does not change the rule; it proves the rule. When you commit adultery or witchcraft, you get death. There are exceptions, but they are exceptions because most of the time there are none.

“O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?” Someone was going into each of the churches where the disciples were teaching, spreading misinformation, confusing and bewitching the congregations. That is infiltration: someone saying I believe, and then teaching something contrary to what they were sent to teach.

“Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?” Did you receive the spirit of Christ by offering animals, or by hearing of Christ? How did you learn the gospel? The works of the law in verse 2 is the law of sacrifice, the same works of the law by which no man is justified in Galatians 2:16.

“Are ye so foolish?” Are you stupid or something? Something wrong with you? Are you slow? Paul is cursing them out. “Having begun in the Spirit”, having begun learning about Christ, “are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” The flesh of animals.
“Have ye suffered so many things in vain?” Are you going through persecution and being hated for following Christ for nothing?

“Doeth he it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?” The works of the law in verse 5 is the same as in verse 2: sacrifice. These are the Christians' go-tos: they run to Galatians 2:16, to 3:2 and to 3:5, and all three go into the same thing.

“Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.” Abraham's faith came first. God told Abraham, I'm going to give you a son, a whole lot of land, and children like the sand of the sea, and Abraham said, all right, sounds good to me. Then he offered sacrifices, after he believed what God told him. His faith came first and God counted that for righteousness, not his offering up an animal. That was secondary.

“They which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham.” The scripture foresaw “that God would justify the heathen through faith”. Heathen is another word for Gentiles: God would justify the Israelites scattered among the Gentiles through faith. “In thee shall all nations be blessed.” Here they say, see, brother, all nations will be blessed. That is twisting the scripture, doing what the Bible says not to do.

Esau already got his blessing: blood and death, weaponry, war, bloodshed, nukes, witchcraft. Isaac blessed Esau; he isn't getting blessed again, and he is dropping his blessings on Iran right now. The blessing for the nations is to work forever: to build up our kingdom and survive the destruction, to be a slave.

“So then they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham”: the Israelites who have faith in Christ are the children of Abraham, who was known for his strong faith.

“For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse”. Those four words again: works of the law, in verse 2, in verse 5, in verse 10 and in Galatians 2:16. They go to the law of sacrifice, Nehemiah 10:33. Under the curse of the covenant: everyone who confirmed to do everything under that covenant, which is offering up animals. If you violate laws that you can't use an animal for, you are cursed: you get death.

“No man is justified by the law in the sight of God”: justified by the works of the law and justified by the law are the same, the same law as in verse 10, verse 5, verse 2 and Galatians 2:16. “The just shall live by faith.”

“The law is not of faith”, because faith came first. “The man that doeth them shall live in them”: the man who does them, offering sacrifice, lives until he commits a sin worthy of death. Then he can't live anymore.

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. Many read right past it. The curse of the law is death: the death we all confirmed and agreed to, and then violated. Being made a curse for us means he died for us. “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”: Christ took that curse on himself when he was hung.
“That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”: on the Israelites among the Gentiles. “That we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

“I speak after the manner of men”: hypothetically speaking, in layman's terms. “Though it be but a man’s covenant”, covenant or testament, which are the same thing, “yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto”. No man can take away from it or add to it: it is written, it is in stone.

“Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ.” The promise passed on to Abraham went on to Christ our king.

“The law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul” the covenant. That law is sacrificial law: the works of the law in verses 2, 5 and 10, and justified by the law in verse 11. Abraham's promise predates the Mosaic law. The Lord promised Abraham a seed, which goes to Christ, and promised him land, before Moses.

“For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise”: if the inheritance came by the sacrifice, the law would supersede the promise. But how can that be, when the promise came first? It can't. “God gave it to Abraham by promise.”

“Wherefore then serveth the law?” What is the purpose of the animal sacrifice? “It was added because of transgressions”: because of the sins within us, to keep us in check, as Romans 5 showed. “Till the seed should come to whom the promise was made”: the sacrifice was added until the seed arrived, and the seed is Christ, the one seed of verse 16. “In the hand of a mediator”: Moses was our mediator.
“Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid”: the promises came first. No law was given which could have given life, because we were sinful by nature.

“But the scripture hath concluded all under sin”. Here they say, see, all nations are under sin. All nations are sinful, yes, but they are not all under sin. Those under sin are the ones under the law: all Israel, Jews and Gentiles. “That the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe”: all Israel.

“Before faith came”, before Christ arrived, “we were kept under the law”. Paul, writing to the Galatians, says we were kept under the law; and the ones under the law are the ones under sin. “Shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed”: kept, shut up, locked into that covenant until Christ came, died, and freed us from it, granting us liberty.

“Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ”. The law that was our schoolmaster is sacrifice. The sacrificing of animals was a foreshadowing of Christ's death, to prepare us for his body and his death. It was temporary, because we would all eventually have been condemned through it: we were too sinful to keep doing it over and over, and grew weary and rebellious behind it. “That we might be justified by faith”: by Christ's death.
“But after that faith is come”, the time of reformation, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster”: no longer under the law of sacrifice.

“For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.” Remember, he said we were kept under the law. All the ye's and you's and our's are the same we that were kept under the law. Don't escape the context: start at verse 23 and read down. “As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ”: the same people who were kept under the law.

“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female”. Christians say it like a soft effeminate man: neither Jew nor Greek, brother; praise white Jesus. They have no idea about the history, so they read it as anybody.

But the ye is the same ye of verse 23 that was kept under the law. Those kept under the law are called Jews and Greeks, bond and free, male and female. The Greeks are Israelites who were made Greeks, as 2 Maccabees shows. So whatever title you go under, free or bond, Jew or Greek, “ye are all one in Christ Jesus”: you are all God's chosen people, whatever your title or status in the world of that time. Paul was free and some were bond, but they were all God's people.
“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” The heirs according to the promise are the Israelites.

precepts.why:
Let's see what “In thee shall all nations be blessed” means. “All the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days.” Then: “Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers”. The ye is the Israelites. Abraham was a prophet, and we are the children of the prophets and of the covenant that passed from Abraham down to Isaac to Jacob.

“Saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.” That is what Galatians 3:8 reads. Then: “Unto you first God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from his iniquities.” Unto you first: the Israelites.

So the blessing is Christ dying for Israelites, for all of us scattered among all the nations. All the kindreds of the earth being blessed is the Israelites scattered abroad being blessed by the death of Christ. We cannot reach all our people on this earth; it is too big. But wherever Israel is scattered, wherever we are found, Christ's blood covers us all. Israel is scattered among the nations and blessed there with the death of Christ: that is what all nations being blessed means.

How do we know who the heathen are that God would justify through faith? “In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.” All the seed of Israel, the families scattered abroad in the earth, are justified by faith in Christ. You will not find anywhere in the law and the prophets that Christ would justify, atone for or reconcile all the heathen Gentile nations through his death.

Show a precept where all the seed of Edom shall be justified, all the seed of Moab, all the seed of Ishmael, all the seed of the Canaanites. Give one place. It isn't anywhere in there. All the seed of Israel shall be justified, whether they are called Jews or called Gentiles, when Christ died for them among the nations.

What does it mean, cursed is he that continueth not to do all that is written in the book? Deuteronomy 27 shows it. “Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image”, “And all the people shall answer and say, Amen.” What happens to him? Can he atone for it, be reconciled with God, find justification? No. Under the old covenant you get death. That is what the curse means.

“Cursed be he that setteth light by his father or his mother”: who disrespects, curses or strikes his mother and father. “And all the people shall say, Amen”: we all agreed to it. Can you atone for it? What animal can you use?

“Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour’s landmark.” Has the so-called white man removed his neighbour's landmark? America is a stolen landmark, Africa is a stolen landmark, Australia is a stolen landmark. How can he atone while the land is still in his possession, sitting on stolen land and killing his brother? He can't.

“Cursed be he that lieth with his father’s wife”, his stepmother: no atonement. “Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast”: a goat, a sheep, a monkey, a fish, a snake, whatever the hell it is; people are weird. “Cursed be he that lieth with his sister”, “Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law”, “Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly”, that kills his brother in secret and doesn't get caught, “Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person”: a hitman, a mercenary. You cannot atone for any of these.

Then “Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them”: that is what Paul quotes in Galatians 3:10. It is death all throughout. Those of the works of the law are under that curse, because they confirmed to do everything under that covenant, offering up animals, and then broke laws no animal can cover.

“Through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: And by him all that believe are justified from all things”. Through Christ is preached the forgiveness of sins, and by him all who believe in Christ's death are justified from all things: all sins.

Could you receive justification from all things under Moses? No, because animals do not atone for all things. Christ's death atones for all things, reconciles us from all things, justifies us from all things. That is the difference: “from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.” That law is the works of the law, sacrifice. That is why no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, and the just shall live by faith.

What is the curse of the law? Death. But a scripture has to back that up. Caiaphas, “being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all, Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” The whole nation: all twelve tribes. That is the curse of the law: all twelve tribes broke the first covenant, and by that default we were all worthy of death. When Christ died, he took that curse upon himself for us.

“He prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; And not for that nation only”, not for Judah only, “but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.” Gather together in one goes back to reconciliation, to at-one-ment, atonement, justification. Christ died for Judah and for Israel, all twelve tribes. Those scattered abroad are the ones Paul was going to, among the heathen, among the Gentiles, while being called Gentiles themselves.

“If a man have committed a sin worthy of death, and he be to be put to death, and thou hang him on a tree: His body shall not remain all night upon the tree”, “for he that is hanged is accursed of God”. Hanging was capital punishment among us. So Christ took the curse for us, the punishment and consequence of violating that covenant, upon himself when he was hung.

Some say he wasn't hung, he was nailed to a cross. If you are nailed to a wooden pole, you are hanging by your hands and feet. That is a lynching. And the lynchings among our people are no coincidence: the white man hung us from trees and lamps and bridges, to a capacity no one else has been hung. Christ died a black man's death.

Peter calls it the same thing: “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.” Hanged on a tree, on a wooden cross. That is how Christ was made a curse for us, as it is written, cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.

Peter says it twice: “And we are witnesses of all things which he did both in the land of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they slew and hanged on a tree”. They hung Christ on a tree, on wood, a cross. He was lynched; he was hung for hours.

“What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin”. The all that the scripture concluded under sin is Jews and Gentiles: Israel called Jews and Israel called Gentiles. All nations are sinful, but they are not all under sin.

“And so all Israel shall be saved”: that is the conclusion of Romans 11. “As it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob”.

“For as ye in times past have not believed God, yet have now obtained mercy through their unbelief”: the northern kingdom obtained mercy, and they that did not believe are the Jews. This is Israel. “Even so have these also now not believed, that through your mercy they also may obtain mercy. For God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all.” Who is them all? All Israel, verse 26.

So who is concluded all under sin, or in unbelief, which is the same thing? All Israel. And the promise by faith of Jesus Christ is given to them that believe: all Israel.

“Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law”. Whatever the law says, it says to those under the law. Who is under the law? The same ones who are under sin. That is the we Paul says was kept under the law.

This is an example of the works of the law. It “was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience”. The gifts and sacrifices could not make the one who did the sacrificing perfect as pertaining to the mind, because sin was already in us since Adam. So the animals had to be temporary.

They “stood only in meats and drinks”, meat offerings and drink offerings, “and divers washings”, which are baptisms, “and carnal ordinances”, the traditions of men, of the Pharisees and them, “imposed on them until the time of reformation.” Imposed, forced upon them. These are the works of the law read all through Galatians 2:16, 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10-11.

The time of reformation is the faith which should afterwards be revealed: until Christ came and did away with all of it. Kept under carnal ordinances, gifts and sacrifices and divers washings, shut up until the time of reformation: the exact same thing Paul says in Galatians 3:23.

Christianity has no idea about history, so they read “neither Jew nor Greek” as anybody. Here is why Paul speaks of Greeks. “Neither was it lawful for a man to keep sabbath days or ancient fasts”. For context: “the king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and not to live after the laws of God”.

Your law, your culture and your race go hand in hand with God. Deny your laws and by default you deny your race. Love your neighbour as yourself: that is law. Deny your race, you deny your laws; deny your law, you deny your God.

It was not lawful “to profess himself at all to be a Jew.” It was illegal by the king's order to call yourself a Jew or keep Jewish customs. So over time we became Greeks, Gentiles.

This is what Jason did, a wicked Israelite. “Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest”. He changed his name to Jason, a Greek name, and sought to make all our people conform to that way of life. He sought underhandedly to be high priest against his brother Onias, a righteous man, by means of money. When a man seeks leadership, he usually isn't meant to be a leader at all.

He promised the king “three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents”: he bribed the king of the Greeks, the white man, to force his brother out of position and put him in authority. Beside that, “he promised to assign an hundred and fifty more, if he might have licence to set him up a place for exercise”, a gym, “and for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen”: the training up of the Israelite youth in the culture of the heathen, here the Greeks, “and to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians.”

The Israelites of Jerusalem were written up as Antiochians, citizens of Antioch, after Antiochus. Jason did it to Hellenize, to Greekify Jerusalem; it was seen as a betrayal of their ancestral laws and a shift toward the Greek way of life, and that tension brought on the Maccabean revolt. Antioch, Turkey: the same Antioch Paul wrote of in Galatians 2:11. So Antiochian and Greek are synonymous: we became Greeks. When Paul says neither Jew nor Greek, he is writing to the descendants of those same people.

Who are the heirs according to the promise? They say all nations. Paul says: “my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh: Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises”. The covenants passed on from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the giving of the law, the service of God that made us the servants of God, and the promises all pertain to Israelites. “Whose are the fathers”: the promises belong to our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and pertain to the Israelites.

“And of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came”: concerning Paul's flesh, his race. Who did Christ come for? Israelites. So the heirs according to the promise in Galatians 3:29 are the Israelites.

sense.text:
Remember the context. The schoolmaster is sacrifice, the works of the law found in Galatians 3:2, 3:5, 3:10-11 and 2:16. If your notes are trash, you'll be confused for a very long time.

“Now I say, That the heir”: the heir here is the same as the heirs according to the promise in Galatians 3:29. “As long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all”. Christ was an heir and a king, and he was a servant. A king has to serve the people. The prince, as long as he is a child, differs nothing from a servant.

“But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father.” A child can't reign right away. He has to be under tutors and governors, mentored, with advisors, to groom him for kingship, until he is grown and ready to sit on the throne. The tutors and governors go back to the schoolmaster of chapter 3. Under Moses we were children, not ready to sit on that throne yet, and the sacrificial law was grooming us for kingship, for Christ.

Under the Mosaic law we were children: sacrifice and sin again, sacrifice and sin again, then into slavery, out of slavery, into slavery again. Stupid kids getting punished and beaten over and over and over again. The Lord said, enough sacrifice; I've got my son down there now. So we were children under a schoolmaster, groomed and mentored for the foreshadowing of Christ's death. The time appointed of the father is the sending of Christ: we were under a schoolmaster until faith came, and the father sent his son to die for us.

“Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world”. Even so: a comparison. We, the heirs of the promise, the Israelites, were children like the heir, in bondage under the elements of the world.

“But when the fulness of the time was come”: back to verse 2, the time appointed of the father. Paul repeats himself. In Paul's letters the answer is usually above the verse, within the verse or under the verse, or it is given more clearly somewhere else, because the same issue was constant throughout the churches, so he addresses it in one church more clearly and in more detail than in another. Those can be precepted together, the letters to the Corinthians with the letters to the Romans, like Romans 14 with 1 Corinthians 8.

“God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law”.

“To redeem them that were under the law”. Christ was born of a woman to redeem them that were under the law. “That we might receive the adoption of sons”: the same we of chapter 3. The adoption pertains to the Israelites.

“And because ye are sons”, the heirs of the promise, “God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son”: when Christ died, we became sons of the Father, “and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.”
“When ye knew not God”, when we sinned against God, “ye did service unto them which by nature are no gods”: we were idolaters.

“But now, after that ye have known God”: now we know the true God, not a pagan one, “or rather are known of God”, because Christ died for us. “How turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements”: verse 3 says the elements of the world, and here they are weak and beggarly elements. “Whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?” The same bondage as verse 3, and as chapter 2, where they desired to bring us back into bondage.

It is said that the works of the law never say the law of sacrifice. But the scripture calls the works of the law bondage, and calls them weak and beggarly elements. The weak and beggarly elements, weak and unprofitable, are the sacrificing of animals.

“Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years.” Paul gives an example of how they had turned back: they were back observing the weak and beggarly elements, the sacrifices of the days, the months, the times and the years.

precepts.why:
Paul said it earlier: “false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage”. Unawares brought in: people were coming in to learn but not really to learn. They were infiltrating. They were brought in and no one knew they were not about the truth, so they came in privily.

Our liberty is Christ dying on the cross and redeeming us out of the death of the old covenant, that the whole nation perish not. The bondage they wanted to bring us back into is the bondage under the elements of the world of Galatians 4:3.

This is the nail in the coffin. “And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament”: Christ is the mediator of the New Testament, not the old. “That by means of death”, by dying for us, hung on the cross, “for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament”. Redemption is the redeeming, the state of redeeming: Christ died for the redeeming of the transgressions that were under the first testament. Who was under the first testament? Israel. So them that were under the law, whom Christ was sent to redeem, are Israel.

What is the weak and beggarly element? “For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh”. The law was weak. It was weak through the flesh: through our sin, through us. And what it could not do was make the conscience perfect, as Hebrews 9:9 shows.

What could the law not do, in that it was weak? The gifts and sacrifices “could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience.” Sacrificing animals could not make us perfect. That is the weakness of the law, and that is the weak element the Galatians were turning back to.

The law could not make the conscience perfect, and it was weak; Galatians calls it the weak and beggarly elements. “For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.” What made the law weak and unprofitable? “For the law made nothing perfect”, including a man's conscience. That is animal sacrifice. The weak and beggarly elements were unprofitable because we were too sinful to keep maintaining them, and they were disannulled. “But the bringing in of a better hope did; by the which we draw nigh unto God”: that is Christ.

“For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.” It never made those who offered them perfect. The weak and beggarly elements are the sacrificing of animals.

This is how they were bewitched. “Certain men which came down from Judea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” After the manner of Moses, sacrifice followed circumcision, on the eighth day. So circumcision after the manner of Moses meant sacrifice, an animal or, for the poor, the flour.

“Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them”, and they went up to Jerusalem about it, because it caused confusion: these men came out from Judea infiltrating and saying the brethren had to sacrifice. Then “there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.” The Pharisees who believed were pushing and imposing sacrifice after the manner of Moses. It says they believed because they were part of the church, yet they brought this in. These are the same false brethren unawares brought in, and that is who Paul is addressing in Galatians.

Be mindful of always saying blood sacrifice, because they will come with that. “And almost all things are by the law purged with blood”. Almost all things: not every sin. Some among our people were poor and could not bring a blood sacrifice.

“But if he be not able to bring two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, then he that sinned shall bring for his offering the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering”. Read the whole chapter: if they could not afford turtledoves or pigeons, it could be flour. “He shall put no oil upon it, neither shall he put any frankincense thereon: for it is a sin offering.” The priest takes “his handful of it, even a memorial thereof, and burn it on the altar, according to the offerings made by fire unto the Lord: it is a sin offering.”

So the works of the law are sacrifice, not only blood. Stay away from saying blood all the time; say sacrifice.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” That was the main example: he that kept the laws of God, that was obedient, brought sacrifice enough. “He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour; and he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.” “To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” Propitiation is reconciliation.

When you depart from sin and keep God's commandments, that is sacrifice enough. Israel didn't get there. Israel thought, I can sin all I want and sacrifice all I want and I'm good. The Lord said, enough of that.

“Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink”: meat offerings and drink offerings, the meats and drinks of Hebrews 9:10. “Or in respect of an holyday”: days. “Or of the new moon”: months. “Or of the sabbath days”: times. “Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” Christ is the body. He is the sacrifice of all those things, because on each of those days a sacrifice had to be made.

Ezekiel 45:17 answers to Colossians 2:16 and Galatians 4:10. “It shall be the prince’s part to give burnt offerings, and meat offerings, and drink offerings, in the feasts”, times and years, “and in the new moons”, months, “and in the sabbaths”, days, “in all solemnities of the house of Israel”, years: “he shall prepare the sin offering, and the meat offering, and the burnt offering, and the peace offerings, to make reconciliation for the house of Israel.”

That was the premise. As the movement of Christ's followers kept growing, the Pharisees were going into the churches trying to win them back to temple law. Paul said he profited in the Jews' religion; that was their bread and butter, people bringing forth animals for sacrifice. They were trying to bring them back into temple law, basically saying to hell with what Christ did, you need an animal atonement. And Paul answers: if you do, you are condemned, because the temple would eventually be destroyed.

sense.text: “Tell me, ye that desire to be under the law”: under the law is the sacrifice, the weak and beggarly elements. “Do ye not hear the law?” Do you not hear what the law says?

“Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman.” The bondmaid is Hagar and the freewoman is Sarah. “He who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh”: that is Ishmael. “He of the freewoman was by promise”: Sarah was promised to bring forth a child in her old age, the child of promise. And the promises pertain to the Israelites.

“These are the two covenants”: the two women stand for two covenants, one for bondage and one for freedom. Hagar is the old covenant; Sarah is the new. “The one from the mount Sinai”, the one that came from Moses, “which gendereth to bondage”: we were bound to offering up animals, and then Christ died, and his death liberated us from that and gave us liberty. Agar is that bondage.

“And answereth to Jerusalem which now is”: Jerusalem maintained the old covenant law, the testament law, “and is in bondage with her children”, in bondage under the Mosaic law, temple law.
“But Jerusalem which is above is free”, because Christ died and we are free from that, “which is the mother of us all.”
“Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not”: this goes to Sarah.
“Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise.” This makes it clear who the Galatians are. Paul calls them brethren, his brothers, and says we are the children of promise as Isaac was.

“He that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the Spirit”: Ishmael mocked Isaac our forefather. “Even so it is now”: the Pharisees mocked the followers of Christ, one toward bondage, one toward freedom.

“Nevertheless what saith the scripture?” Despite the persecution: “Cast out the bondwoman and her son”. Get the old covenant out of here, and her son, those who maintain that sacrificial law. “For the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman.” We are the sons of the free woman.

It is twofold. The old covenant is done away with and the new is in. And the son of the bondwoman, the children of the flesh, are not getting the kingdom along with us either. They are not the heir; we are the heirs, the children of promise. No fleshly heathens are getting our inheritance.
“So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free”: the children of promise.

precepts.why: Who was Paul writing to in Galatians, for the Christians still confused, secretly spying out the liberty we have in Christ? “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia”. Galatia. The strangers scattered throughout Galatia are the “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”: the death of Christ.

To these same strangers: “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people”. The strangers of Galatia are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation. “Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.”

So the Galatians were Israelites, primarily the northern kingdom, who had accepted Christ and were being deceived, and whom Paul reasoned with in his letter. They are the children of the free woman, the children of promise.
